It causes that which has not yet arisen to arise, and once arisen, it causes it to continue in succession.
If sentient beings have already planted roots of goodness and have already eliminated all obstacles, [it brings them to maturity].
Although they have already been able to mature the accumulations of merit and knowledge,
because they have not yet eliminated their attachments,
they have not yet realized the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I have taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature,
neither arising nor ceasing, primordially quiescent,
and by their very nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
If sentient beings have already planted roots of goodness,
have already eliminated all hindrances, and have already perfected their provisions,
they belong to the category of wisdom and not to the category of folly.
Upon hearing me teach this dharma of selflessness,
they are able to accept it with faith, correctly understand the Buddha’s intent,
practice in accordance with reality, and remain free from attachment.
One realizes the ultimate peace and bliss of nirvana;
this dharma, which is without intrinsic nature and free from arising and ceasing,
brings about great benefit for that person.
If sentient beings have not yet planted roots of goodness,
have not yet extinguished their various hindrances,
and have not yet completed their accumulations of merit and wisdom.
Having heard my teaching that all these phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are subject to neither arising nor ceasing,
they are able to accept it with faith, yet they cannot skillfully understand the intended meaning of what was said;
consequently, they adhere to it with fixed attachment.
From such attachment, the view of annihilation arises;
clinging to the notion that all phenomena are truly devoid of intrinsic nature and so forth,
one is unwilling to practice any wholesome dharmas.
They do not plant roots of goodness nor extinguish their various obscurations;
they are unable to bring to maturity the provisions of merit and wisdom,
and they slander all phenomena that possess intrinsic nature.
Because it destroys all roots of merit and virtue,
this profound and wondrous Dharma of lack of intrinsic nature brings about great ruin for such a person.
The scriptural text is extremely extensive and its purport is broadly dispersed;
therefore, at this time, I shall explain by exploring its underlying meaning.
Since the sublime teaching is clearly manifest, it may be relied upon as a foundation.

As it might become overly cumbersome to explain this in full detail, I shall respond briefly to the twenty-first question, which asks: "Regarding the ālayavijñāna and the Great Wisdom, although they differ in being turbid and clear, are they one or are they different? What is the meaning of this? I respectfully reply: They are neither identical nor distinct. Why? Because the nature of the ālayavijñāna is fundamentally pure; it is only due to adventitious defilements that it appears turbid.

Just as water is inherently clear but becomes turbid when stirred by wind, so too is the ālayavijñāna inherently pure, yet it appears turbid through the influence of ignorance and afflictions. When these adventitious defilements are removed, its original clarity is revealed. Therefore, in terms of their ultimate essence, there is no difference between them; they are one and the same. However, in terms of their phenomenal manifestations, they appear as two: one is the state of delusion and obscuration, and the other is the state of awakening and luminosity. Thus, while they are non-dual in substance, they are distinguished by their modes of appearance. This is the meaning.
The ālayavijñāna is the ālaya;
it is the tathāgatagarbha for those of great wisdom,
because it possesses the nature of the radiance of great wisdom.
Although clarity and turbidity differ, their nature and characteristics are difficult to distinguish.
Speaking from this perspective, they are neither identical nor distinct.
Thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states in a verse based on this:
The Tathāgata’s pure storehouse and the worldly *ālayavijñāna* are mutually indistinguishable, like gold and a ring.
The analogy of gold and a ring illustrates the relationship between the Tathāgatagarbha and the *ālayavijñāna*.
This is the meaning of neither identity nor difference.
Regarding "neither identity nor difference," as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
A lump of clay and its subtle particles are neither identical nor different;
it is the same with gold and its ornaments.
That is to say, the entirety of the gold constitutes the finger-ring.
Therefore, gold and the ring are neither identical nor different.
If gold and the ring were one and the same,
then when the appearance of the ring ceases, the substance of the gold should also cease.
If the characteristic of the ring were to perish while the substance of the gold did not perish,
then one could not say that the gold and the ring are identical.
If the gold and the characteristic of the ring were different, [then...]
How could the characteristic of the ring exist apart from the gold?
Nor can one seek the essence of the gold separately from the ring.
Thus, the gold and the characteristic of the ring are established as being neither identical nor different.
One should know that the same applies to the *ālayavijñāna* and wisdom (*jñāna*).
The *tathāgatagarbha* is the true mind,
whereas the *ālaya* is the deluded consciousness.
The true mind in its purity is the original source;
deluded consciousness, subject to arising and ceasing, constitutes the cycle of wandering.
Although this is the general explanation, to distinguish them specifically:
This refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamental true mind.

Although its nature is pure, eternally abiding, and unconditioned, it does not remain fixed in its original stillness; thus, it is perfumed by ignorance and moved, thereby forming deluded consciousness.
Following the flow of birth and death, one becomes a sentient being;
yet, though becoming a sentient being, one does not lose one's fundamental nature.
Therefore, by departing from deluded consciousness, one returns to the original source.
If the *tathāgatagarbha* maintains its nature of eternal permanence,
it does not incur the fault of the extreme of asserting that sentient beings are permanent;
yet, when the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests as sentient beings...
If one loses its fundamental nature, there is the fault of falling into the extreme of annihilation;
since the Tathāgatagarbha is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Therefore, it is neither identical to nor different from deluded consciousness.
If they were definitively identical, then when deluded consciousness ceases, the true mind would also cease;
this would constitute the extreme of annihilationism.
If they were definitively distinct,
then when the deluded consciousness moves, the true mind would remain unmoved;
this would entail falling into the extreme of eternalism.
Because these two are extremes, they are neither identical nor different.
The reason for the question is established according to the Dharma-nature school (Faxiang zong),
while the framework addressed therein is established according to the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao).
This differs slightly from the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) and other such systems;
the fundamental tenets are distinct, which I humbly request you to examine clearly.
The twenty-second question states:

"When the Buddha was in the world, the community of monks practiced a single Dharma together; yet after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it divided into four schools, differing from one another. Among these four schools, what is that single Dharma? I respectfully respond.
When the Buddha was in the world, he was the Great Teacher who guided the world;
his true influence spread far and wide, and the rain of Dharma fell in profusion.
All together received the teachings of the Compassionate Honored One, having no other master or model.
The Great Earth destroys the path through the Dharma-gate of non-duality;
the Small Vehicle follows the way with unified knowledge and vision.
There are no divergent tracks, as all alike receive and follow thorough penetration.
By the time [the Buddha] awakened and returned to the truth, demonic influences were rampant, sentient beings lost their footing, and the True Dharma declined;
consequently, the single-flavored Dharma was divided into various schools of views, and the subtle words of the Tripiṭaka [were obscured].
The mouths of the deluded masses were silenced, yet they vied with one another to proclaim their own divergent paths.
Teachers and disciples each harbored mutual resentment and aversion;
as they further aligned themselves in factions and shifted allegiances, sectarian attachments first began to take root.

The title "Twenty" became widely circulated for a long time, yet it was commonly heard that there were only four or five [chapters]. Regarding what was said about the "four": (Note: This passage reflects a historical observation concerning the transmission of a specific Buddhist text—likely the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* or a related commentary—where the title "Twenty" (referring to twenty chapters) persisted despite the fact that only four or five chapters were actually extant or recognized by some traditions.)
This refers to the Western Regions,
where each possesses its own Tripitaka and the four schools of thought are widely practiced.
1. The Sthavira school;
2. The Sarvāstivāda school;
3. The Mahāsāṃghika school.
The fourth is the Saṃmitīya school.
As for what is called the "five schools," these are those of the East.
However, regarding the Vinaya school, there are five divisions.
The first is the Sarvāstivāda,
namely the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), which appears to be practiced in the land of Han.
Second is the Dharmaguptaka,
namely the *Four-Part Vinaya* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya), which is widely prevalent in the land of Han.
Third is the Mahīśāsaka.
Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* was practiced little in the land of Han;
as for the four *Mahāsāṃghika* [vinayas],
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was not used in the land of Han.
The five Kāśyapīya schools transmitted the Vinaya of emptiness;
each possessed only the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
These five schools of the East came from the Western Regions.
The four schools of the Western Regions all transmit that this text originally existed;
they all claim it was spoken by the Buddha and unanimously designate it as the "Sacred Word.
Now, one must clarify the origins and development of its existence.
The initial emergence of the sects resulted in twenty distinct schools;
yet, as transmitted through the ages, only four or five remain.
First, I shall clarify the reasons for the names of these twenty schools.
Next, regarding the similarities and differences among the four or five teachings,
as for what is called the "twenty schools," the Mañjuśrī Sūtra states:
The eighteen [sects] and the two original ones both emerged from the Great Assembly.
There is neither "is" nor "is not"; I say they will arise in the future.
Regarding what are called the "two original ones," there are two layers.
Twelve years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Mahākāśyapa contemplated the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka;
he struck Mount Sumeru and proclaimed to all:
"May the noble ones not enter parinirvāṇa.
A Dharma assembly shall be held in Rājagṛha;
at that time, the assemblies of noble ones from the four continents will all gather there."
King Ajātaśatru offered lavish provisions for seven days.
After the seven days had passed, Mahākāśyapa, fearing that the large number of people would make it difficult to accomplish the Dharma-rite,
selected five hundred noble monks who were beyond training (aśaikṣa), who had mastered the Tripitaka, and who were possessed of great learning.
He sat in retreat during the rains-retreat at the Saptaparṇa Cave;
during the first three months of the rainy season, he compiled the Tripiṭaka,
the first of which is the Sūtra.
Second, the Vinaya;
third, the Abhidharma.
Among the other assemblies, there are likewise those who are proficient in all three Piṭakas.
Having been selected for dismissal, they lamented together, saying:
"While the Tathāgata was still in the world, we were of one teacher and shared the same filial devotion;
now that the Dharma King has entered parinirvāṇa, he has singled us out for exclusion."
Wishing to repay the Buddha’s kindness, he should collect the Dharma-piṭaka.
Outside that cave, in a secluded forest, he sat for the rainy season retreat and compiled the five piṭakas;
to the previous three, he added the Mantra-piṭaka and the Miscellaneous-piṭaka.
Initially, they were called the Sthavira (Elders) because the senior monk among Kāśyapa’s community was named Sthavira;
later, they were called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) because ordinary and noble beings resided together.
This constitutes their first fundamental division.
Once the collection was completed, they each memorized and upheld the two Dharma-piṭakas according to their own preferences, without contradicting one another’s sequence.
More than a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the time since the Sage had passed was as long as the sun had already set.
In the kingdom of Magadha, at the city of Kusumapura, there was a king named Aśoka who ruled over Jambudvīpa. Moved by compassion,
he manifested a single white parasol that brought cooling relief to both humans and deities.
At that time, the great assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was divided;
that is to say, because the fourfold assembly held differing opinions regarding the five points of Mahādeva, they split into two schools.
As for what is called the "fourfold assembly":
First, the assembly of nāga-elephants;
second, the assembly of the various schools;
third, the assembly of those of great learning.
Regarding the assembly of the four virtues:
as for the one called Mahādeva,
there was a merchant in the kingdom of Mathurā.
He married a young wife and fathered a son of upright countenance named Mahādeva. Meanwhile,
the merchant Hañña had remained long in another country.
When the son had reached full maturity, his mother pressured him to depart in haste.
Later, hearing that his father had returned, he was filled with fear;
he devised a plan with his mother and subsequently murdered him by administering poison.
Fearing that their deeds would soon become manifest, they fled together to another country;
wandering from place to place to escape the danger, they arrived at Pāṭaliputra,
